title: Material Science Laboratory Documentation
text:
1 Introduction
(To the Material Science and Computational Modelling (AI & Modelling))
Welcome, to the research documentation page on material science and such applications or investigations using artificial intelligence, for the lack of better work downgrading current infrastructures to, and computational simulation, without restriction to simple binary simulation itself. Our purpose in such research is then fairly simple to state. More specifically, what we want includes:

Investigation of the foundational concepts, constructs, models, realization, assumption, oracle specification, truncated regions, meaning, and so on when in consideration of physics, to subject as specific of materials and their structural consequences.
We study the intrinsic image and realization of different models as such in material science, from which we identify of the structural error, region of fallacy, failure modes and so on that instead of entangle the system in a network of patchwork, we diagnose specific pattern and junctions where analysis on multi-angle model cohesion can be achieved. Within such, perhaps proposal for new models or a unified one can be attained.
We study the close problem between theoretical-practical gap of material science on paper and of its instantiation, for also computer simulation models.
Within it, we study simulation theory in close quarter to material science, the simulated problem on the inability to capture many-body physics without using upper-layer zoom-out measure (statistics and quantum mechanics are admission of such that the details are either too complex, or too unknown to be grounded specifically). The gap is then also between described construction and admitted structures, in which we are to realize on the method to simulate a structure more than just numerical computation, and furthermore on the disadvantage, compartment removal in such method of simulating under constraints.
Using AI, or rather, applying AI toward specific structural purposes, we probe the usage of AI-like system for the lack of analysis thereof, to see their applications, inherited or extracted features, the fitting patterns that they design or extrapolated, and furthermore the inherent limitation they carry. Ever more specifically, if we are to treat AI system as tangible for realization of material science structure, we ought to also realize what they capture and how the semantic dynamic structure is moved in-between of the AI substrates.

With such, our goal is rather large. The first section perhaps would cover the more basic of material science, as a survey into within itself of the field, and further more if time and resource is allowed. Nevertheless, within such a long plan, we are to fill it with not buzzword but actual concepts. For the lack of word and the abundance thereof being superficial teleology, we are to say the words toward what they are worth.
This is inherited, or born out of participation of the Computational Material Science Laboratory. Following up of such, I thank for their guidances thereof.

title: 2  Material
text:
2.1 The tell-tale of material (Amelia Carolina Sparavigna, 2011)
Before studying anything about material science, we might as well be familiarized of the concept, and the historiography on what material can be constituted of. Surprisingly, or rather the unsurprising thereof, is that such concept has been presented in a very long time, ever since the old age of the Roman Empire, and further down the path.
In the age of Ancient Rome, two books, the De Architectura by Vitruvius and naturalis Historia by Pliny the Elder, gives us the portrait of the material science, or the knowledge in specificity about materials, in Rome at the beginning of the Empire. In most of the case studies, it is in the making of four case studies: concretes, coatings, amorphous materials, and colloidal crystals, to describe them in the modern corpora of words.
The word science itself comes from the Latin scientia, for which to mean “knowledge”, and then, to find the material science of the past, it is natural to respond it toward the “knowledge of materials”. Interestingly, such knowledge as seen of the use cases, often accompanied us within which our life interacts of it. Such is why, the question of material science in those times are not rather fundamental, but before the requirement of the body of studies, one ask:
Often, the thought of the existence thereof, of being, is reserved to the philosopher as their inquiry requires a form of entanglement and in-depth observations. Though, it does not bring about much in short or medium-term of meaningful actions, such is also why typically, the equation of which we draw about material science would not include that (however, we do note such are rather useful, and would be nice to get).
Most observations about dust and stones thereof, started rather mundanely.
The template of the material presentation is deliberate. Such is where the construct is typical, for Vitruvius to describe pozzolana, derived from unconsolidated pyroclastic materials, of which are now known of such name though unpacking it requires rather substantial time and evidences, erupted by the Campi Flegrei, a volcanic field near Vesuvius. The part is rather interesting - if such is mixed with lime and rubble, it hardens as well under water as in ordinary buildings. Under their civilization perspective, such is rather interesting, because it is basically a type of constructive medium in which can be used to build, of course, building or any form of structures. They are purely of use, and of which their description finds themselves into where the material can be found, and of which such context on where it is found gives rise to the interpretation on the question for how. Such is the same reasoning that would be met of many ancient civilizations, or even modern time of any construct with the lack of structural details, if there is any, and interpretation varies. Interestingly, Vitruvius continues telling that
Even by then, the science of material science constitutes the knowledge on how they are manipulated of form, either by their creation on circumstances speculated, or by artificial means. The process of which describe how the material is formed, by Vitruvius’ word, is rather deliberate, as to mean of a natural fabricating process. Mundane enough to extract the macroscopic properties on ‘how would such operate’, and why. But not enough to say all of it. In essence, the scribe describes the “dissimilar and unequal actions, concentrating the motion towards the same end, the great want of moisture quickly supplied by water binds and strongly cements them, and also imparts a rapid solidity.” per the mechanism of the material. However,
The model does break. Perhaps rather trivially of sort. The property of land, of which forms the basic foundational substrate where this rather derivative form of material can be found, varies between lands, contexts, and regions. The model is thus rather local - it might seem obvious that way, but only under some very specific circumstances that it should rather would be instantiated correctly to give such result. By description of the process, assuming the process is actualization of the real oracle in which how pozzolana is, the actualization requires many contexts of which can be known, or rather not known of, and of conditions and expectations that would happen at will. Moreover, the main assumption of the model is as to always observe the end-product to be pozzolana, of which evidently by his own words, we can take a measured stance as to be not quite. Thus, such concludes the written description of the first “hydraulic cement” in history. Such is not perfect, nor it is anywhere near what we have, but their process is the same - the model breaks under instantiation of context, works within what it describes, and of which for the details it is given, and assumptions on what observe, deliver the interpretation befit of replication to a given degree.
Such can be said of many problems and models we currently use in history of science as to the modern time. While technology have advanced, technology in itself is the utlization of such, and thus bares the same notion in which manipulation and knowledge is rather not perfect, as to there exist many failure points one cannot expect. One can also find utilization, crude but effective way of such in Pliny’s cement, of which the human industry devised even broken pottery into something else. Most of them have the virtue of the generous context. We, however, do not.

Marcus Vitruvius Pollio lived in the 1st century BC. He was a Roman architect and engineer, best known as the author of the “De Architectura” [5]. Gaius Plinius Secundus, known as Pliny the Elder, died on 25 August, 79 AD during the eruption of Mount Vesusius. He was a Roman naturalist as well as naval commander of the Roman Empire. He wrote an encyclopaedic work, the “Naturalis Historia” [6]. These two books give us a portrait of knowledge in Rome, at the beginning of the Empire, and deserve a longer study. For instance, the “Naturalis Historia” contains several detailed descriptions of metals, pigments and precious stones.



There is a species of sand which, naturally, possesses extraordinary qualities. It is found about Baiae and the territory in the neighbourhood of Mount Vesuvius; if mixed with lime and rubble, it hardens as well under water as in ordinary buildings. This seems to arise from the hotness of the earth under these mountains and the abundance of springs under their bases. (Vitruvius, translated)



[…] it seems certain that the moisture is extracted from the sand-stone and earth in their neighbourhood, by the strength of the fire, as from limestone in a kiln. Dissimilar and unequal actions thus concentrated towards the same end, the great want of moisture quickly supplied by water binds and strongly cements them, and also imparts a rapid solidity.



But he notes that in Tuscany, where there are several hot springs too, “we do not there find a powder, which, for the same reason, would harden under water … All lands do not possess similar qualities; nor is stone universally found. Some lands are earthy, others gravelly, others gritty, others sandy: in short, the quality of land, in different parts of the earth, varies as much as even the climate itself.”

section: 2.2 The modern history of material science
text:
2.2 The modern history of material science
Due of history, material science emerged full-fledged in the USA, some time in the early 1950s. However, the period before it stems much of the context into which the current structure of material science is of present. And a fairly dirty history one can get from it. Per Mody and Martin (2020) for example, such is rather famously taken of a complicated history at large.
Material science stems from, or rather inherited of the settled practices toward what metallurgy is, which have been in existence for a rather long period of time. During the 18th-19th centuries of the enlightenment, knowledge about materials, specifically if we are to host an operational form on what constitutes a material. Traditionally, material in consideration is this solid, but the wider range can be pointed to any form of matter in hosting all state of matters, or now so we speak. In such it also includes, obviously, foundational matters of biological one, so to speak.
There, we gradually gain the empirical ground on metallurgy, chemistry, mechanical engineering, and industrial manufacturing. Per Cahn (2001) and Eliade (1956), of which gives many craft knowledge and scientific investigation of the substrate itself, but not by much being the field of material science. That is because, there exists no middle ground on theories at that focal point, so much so material investigations were solely considered as to be the instantiation of the physical theories and thereof, most often the very general foundational theory of physics. Many would say that material science did not exist before 1950s, and such would be hard to refute.

2.2.1 Cold War reorganization
During the Cold War, the entire field was considered and rather transformed into being of existence, taking on specific pipelines, and body of theories starting from source materials into the actual objects.

Through the mid-1950s, Cold War competition focused principally on nuclear weapons development as the United States and the Soviet Union raced to amass larger and larger arsenals. But within the logic of nuclear deterrence, the delivery systems for nuclear weapons mattered just as much as the weapons themselves. A nation with powerful enough rockets could deliver a nuclear warhead to any spot it chose on the globe. The Soviet launch of the world’s first artificial satellite, Sputnik, on October 4, 1957, therefore represented a shift. The aluminium sphere’s radio blips were not as consequential as the demonstration of rocketry powerful enough to launch a satellite into space—or deliver a nuclear warhead. Some nuclear capabilities would still be based on nuclear-armed aircraft, and later submarines, but an increasing proportion of the nuclear powers’ arsenals would sit on the tip of sophisticated rockets, ready to race toward their targets at a moment’s notice.

Born out of metallurgy (for details, see Cahn (2001)), material science was considered a superdiscipline, as it hinges on very much the entire landscape of science at large of the moment, stretching of all apparatus, theories of all scales, and thus encompassing an unusual interdisciplinary environment condition. The reorganization of material science defines the field by modern standard as to be certainly a pluralism of details

David Turnbull, in his illuminating Commentary on the Emergence and Evolution of “Materials Science” (Turnbull 1983), defined materials science “broadly” as “the characterisation, understanding, and control of the structure of matter at the ultramolecular level and the relating of this structure to properties (mechanical. magnetic, electrical, etc.). That is, it is ‘Ultramolecular Science’.”

or, in one way or another in COSMAT Report of 1974, as

[…] concerned with the generation and application of knowledge relating the composition, structure, and processing of materials to their properties and uses.

During the mid-1950s, there existed at that time, two traditions that would rather unable to talk with one another. First, was the industrial research sector, exemplified by Bell Laboratories, and so forth, but not limited to of legacy, per individual empiricisms without foundation of the Bessemer process (1856), the Siemens-Martin open-hearth furnace (1860s), the Hall-Héroult aluminium process (1886). This only comes back and forth toward temporal inversion - technology precedes theory, theory then rationalizes technology - will soon be observed again pre-formation as such. Bell Lab functioned as more of an industrial research system rather than the typical conventional laboratory that you would see, operating inside a vertically integrated telecommunications monopoly that treated discovery as infrastructure, perhaps more than just some patents. The purposes were not to chase products or market timing but to solve fundamental problems that would stabilize and extend a national communication network, which in turns the monopoly money being reinvested into more foundational problem. Such created of itself an insulating internal culture that permits Bell Laboratory to get the transistor (1947), information theory (1948), laser partly of itself, and so on, and shield them from having to chase external peer review or annual grant cycles, nor commercially relevant products’ formation. As such, we say, that science precedes the commercial utilization.
The other sector was the academic disciplinary science, which is the traditional one where metallurgy grown out of mining engineering curricula were positioned. Working on rather a practical and empirical side, solid-state physics, ceramic engineering, polymer chemistry, and so on, they are settled, at the time, to live in separate buildings, separate departments, using only foundational physics as justification, separate conferences, trained in separate PhD programs, and all of the above. These communities were intellectually productive but siloed, and each was, in Paul Forman’s phrasing, partly insulated from the guiding hand of physics — meaning that engineering-oriented metallurgists and ceramicists were not strongly connected to the theoretical advances in quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics that, in retrospect, were directly relevant to their problems, but without a different eye on the paper sheet.
One example can be filled deliberately, is within the organic and inorganic chemistry of which came into an ever-increasing conflict throughout the nineteenth century, and “indeed as recently as 1969 an eminent British chemist was quoted as asserting that ‘inorganic chemistry is a ridiculous field’”. Both sides are rather deliberately correct on their own, and far wrong on the others, with understanding of what was going on internally of the synthesis of compounds and compositional analysis, specifically on carbon-based structures of organic chemistry and the possibility of the lack thereof, from the inorganic one, remained bedevilled by a number of confusions, “for instance, between gaseous atoms and molecules, the absence of such concepts as stereochemistry and isomerism”. Even right now, the scale problem is particularly absent, to say that chemistry itself did not organize the field within scales and frames in which operatives from foundational primitives are sufficed to characterize which phenomena belong to where, and of what precursor that gives rise to such process, either multi-layer leaks on local-global interaction or not. Unsurprisingly, during such period, there was no agreed atomic theory, and even uncertainty about atomic weights, especially the inorganic elements. Even by now, such problem remains in practice of interaction, as for while there exists the standard model, interactions and dynamics of nuclear physics largely depends on a rather unpleasant proliferation of concepts and pluralism of patchwork models, that is used to understand nucleic interactions and productions.

Another thing to note, lies rather in the physics itself. During the earlier development of metallurgy, during the 1920s, for example with Frenkel’s paper (Frenkel 1926), established what was then known as the plastic deformation paradox. Within such, Frenkel estimated the stress required to slide one atomic plane over another in a perfect lattice and thus gave \[
\tau_{ideal}\approx \frac{G}{2\pi}
\] where \(G\) is the shear modulus. For typical metals, this gives \(\tau_{ideal}\sim 10^{-1}G\), however, experimental yield stresses were typically \(\tau_{exp}\sim 10^{-4}G\). Thus, there exists the discrepancy of the theory itself, and what the experiment gives. By the late 1920s, the discrepancy between theory and experiment of such was widely recognized in crystal physics and metallurgy, for which it is rather troubling because the predictions stemming from such rather suspiciously stable theory can be catastrophically wrong. Such stemmed the efforts made by which is the recognition for dislocation theory, for the specifically jointed tension effort by (Orowan 1934), (Polanyi 1934), then (Taylor 1934) and empirically confirmed of the conjecture by (Hirsch, Horne, and Whelan 2006). where one posits that plastic deformation occurs through line defects than uniform sliding of entire planes. Essentially turning them to local (relatively) events. More specifically, it reframes the entire stress deformation as

A dislocation is a linear crystallographic defect whose motion allows atoms to slide at low stress.

And then, such was used throughout for the theory itself. However, even within such, inconsistency remains between continuum plasticity theory and microscopic dislocation dynamics. This is partially because the interpretation apparatus considered of those structures and theories are entangled, for one is concerned with smooth fields condensation for deformation on continuum, and one defines them via discrete avalanche-like events. The dislocation theory itself carries its fair share of paradox, for example, the paradox of strength and ductility, per (Valiev et al. 2002), for which refers to the difficulty of achieving both high strength and high ductility in materials. A rather more catastrophic one is the Frank-Read source, for which is the mechanism for generation of multiple dislocation in well-spaced slip planes in crystalline structures, under deformation. Even with a recent 2024 papers, they only demonstrated the aspect of empirical deformation under multiplication dislocations. The issue remains that a perfect crystal, initially contains very few dislocations, yet during plastic deformation gives huge density of such. So, where do dislocations come from? Such require jumping outside the framework itself, of which then arguably confusing as to question its own ontology. Which might as well never work. Such also brings about the recent (quite so?) discovery of the severe plastic deformation paradox, which can be seen in (Valiev 2003), and persisted ever since.

Within such systematic decoupling, of the academic field and the industry, the alignment of interests and system default, it is rather not surprising to see the developments failed in a way or another. While one party goes on one way, the other emphasizes another aspect of such. While Bell Laboratory, and many powerhouses of industrial research purposes were given freedom and exploratory merits that feed back to the grinding halt of the private proprietary claims, the other side is largely institutional, fragmented, argued of each other while given no quarter for actual communication and coherence of analysis. Academic tradition was often considered building knowledge for its own sake, organized around disciplinary identity and themed discussion, not allowing for anything else than internal peer recognition and specialties of identity, while the industrial one forgone any kind of theoretical scientific notion, in pursuits of empirical but successful products. The only problem at that point, is the lack of communication between the two, and the internal problem that crippled dialogues from within.
When Sputnik launched in October 4th, 1957, the dialogue switched dramatically into overdrive. It is by then observed of those under administration roles to see of such dilemma, insufficient understanding of materials represented of the 1950s directly to a strategic shortcoming. We do have novel material per se, we do have many wonderful architectural designs. But we do not have a coherent theory, a stable framework, or any form of practical identification or practical theory of sort. Materials Advisory Board’s 1967 report outlined some of such - characterization of material is a bottleneck (and may right now still be within its large complex structures without structural conditions), material construction identification is also a problem, effective theory and usage of materials of the time is mostly unknown, and perhaps furthermore, the practical-theoretical gap is strictly hierarchical officially - where practical knowledges serve to be the second-order of what of the constitution. Utilizing such, the response was framed by specific ideological commitment, of which (Mody and Martin 2020) specified and identified as decisive - many scientists, most specifically American-Western scientists of physics in general, valorized ‘pure science’ and sought to distant themselves from such practical outcomes of their work. Physicists, those of whom are apart from the realization in the physical world, convinced the administrators and generals that engineering is not there sufficient anymore, such is to say paving way for the physics to be of higher-order, and metallurgy, production science, plastic science, to be simply not capable. This, is rather a self-serving framing for physicists - it positioned physics as master science that would redeem the backward engineering fields. That said, the most productive materials research of the preceding decades had come not from physicists imposing their framework on metallurgists and those manufacturing of their own practical devices, but to get the environment similar to Bell Labs, where there exists no clear hierarchy rather than the instantiation thereof, of the distance to be none, that a singular problem can be argued from both side and work on the same range, without the relationship being hierarchical. Such explains of the interdisciplinary failures, the failure of cumulative pluralism, internal disciplinary acceptance of which is rather counterproductive on its own, and the rigidity of expression and backward incompatibility the field inherited parts of.


2.2.2 To the present day
This section is here for now only to serve as the self-serving opening to the next sections. That is rather trivial, because we aim toward clarify the problems inherent of the current structures. Those, and of the fragmentation we would be seeing, came from a long line of slow decays, most often than not the fault of, or not, of the field itself.

title: 3  The map of material science
text:
3.1 Pre-material science
From what we have listed after which the Cold War happened, it is easy to get yourself lost in the land of which material science bases itself in. Indeed of such, the phase right now of history can be considered of the proliferation of the old day material science, much to the disdain of the practitioners standing inside it. Before studying in details of what to entail of the development thereof, we might as well consider the map of material science, from the relative ancient age to the present, and settle a few definitions, operationally speaking that will evolute within times.
The history has not been so kind to the precursors of material science on itself. During much course of histories, material science has been staying in the lane of intriguing but disfranchising field of accumulated research, specifically targeting certain parts of the material landscape. The definition of material, even up to present, is largely incoherent thereof, that it would be difficult to classify of what to be material, as some may even argue that water is a type of material, or it can be a solvent, or it can be a neutral medium. But it just so happens that the current landscape of material science, as of in the past, remains the same. The concept of material has never been given a rigorous, stable and agreed definition across the traditions that constitute materials science. The definition has changed rapidly, repeatedly, each change reflecting a different commitment, not realization, not unification or reverse calibration, but rather to about what kinds of things exist and what kinds of relations between things are scientifically fundamental, if such is even possible thereof.
History of pre-material science can be separated into the concept word of matter. Before the Greek philosophical tradition formalized the concept of matter, there was already a practical concept of material that craftsmen used, shaped and transformed. Those are of the precursor materials, specifically, bronze, iron, clay wood, flax, ivory, stone, and so on. How do they feel of those? Specifically through crude inference, where one makes it so that their property is reflected by a certain metric of utilization or interaction. For example, one can say between bronze and iron, there exists a specific kind of hardness in contact with others, the hardness of manipulation, extraction, and sleight of handling. Cyril Stanley Smith, noted in 1968 that material is the matter of which have been through a relation toward human practice and use, most often so. This practical, relational conception of material was the implicit framework of artisans, craftsmen, and metallurgists from antiquity through the early modern period, much to the disdain of those requiring a more fundamental concept. But even so, it makes sense - matter exists as the wider universal encompassing dilemma of which everything would follow in. Even human exists of matter. Aether, luminiferous aether of the mechanical aether of sort, in which light was supposed to travel in-between, also uses the concept of matter. The Maxwell field equations specifically targetting \((\mathbf{E},\mathbf{B})\) conjunctive fields are also a form of ‘matter’, if we are to speak of the same criteria 1. The problem and difficulty there of, lies in the consequence - it means that the same substance can be simultaneously a material in one context and matter in another - it depends on the anthropological baseline of whatever using it. Such is rather very centric toward the craftsmen, but we soon realized that the world is not only us. The difficulty and the quest to find such, begins with this relational, context-dependent concept and forcing it to the becoming of being universal, of which we might as well say to be independent. We constitute the first act:
Up to another region of time, or so we speak of, Thales of Miletus regarded water as sole fundamental building block of matter, and thus henceforth also material itself. He held that water, in taking different forms, constitutes the earth, atmosphere, sky, mountains, gods and men, beasts and birds, grass and trees, and animals down to worms, flies and ants. All these are different forms of water, and for certainty many of such different qualities inside many matter or materials, would be derivation simply by manipulating water, of which is the ability we do not possess of the time (yet).
This constitutes the second action, the action of fumdamentalizing derivation. Basically speaking, this requires the think that there exists, out of all set \(\{\mathrm{Ma},\mathrm{Me}\}\) for material and matter of arbitrary choice on classification notion (where we can still take the anthropological definition for material), to have certain initial form that would make up literally everything else in existence, just with more details or more complex types. That is, the minimal framework itself. It is understandable how Thales would have thought of such - consider water, a fluid as we know of now, where shape can be transformed, the basis of life and what human (anthropological basis, mind you) cannot live without, the solvent of many processes, medium for many mechanical or proto-chemical purposes. All of such constitutes to the big picture of that water is fundamental, and we cannot really fail that to a given degree of sort.
The problem with Thales’s choice - water - however, is immediately visible. If water is the fundamental substance of all things, then the water being drunk, the water that is flowing in a river, the water sitting in a bowl, the water flowing in rivers, all of which would be equally material in the most basic sense, it serves the purpose of being the functionally invariant structure. But what about iron or any form of metals? Iron cannot be water in any obvious sense. True, that up to now molecular structures can be recombined, and perhaps we can use them to make iron, but that is still excruciatingly hard, and most of the time not even worth the time to do such. Thales must have held that iron is somehow a transformation of water, water to be in a very different form. This means transforming the definition of water to be distant from its normal usage, to something of which is not water but the description of fluid, that is,
But this then fails when you encounter oil, or anything of such form. At that point, you have proliferation of origin - what to be called as the initials, oil or water? A sidestep can also happen if we get the Second Thales of Miletus - regarding a substance \(X\) to be the unified form of which iron can be made of its derivation. But it just so happens that there are also many forms of things that look like iron, but does not act like iron in any form. This again, means pluralism of definition and the redefinition stack of which will dilute the meaning of the origin to be said of.
Coincidentally or not based on our projection, this is the first appearance of a pattern that will recur throughout the entire history - the concept chosen as fundamental for “material” turns out to require extensive redefinition in order to accommodate everything it needs to accommodate, until the word means something quite different from its ordinary usage, while the ordinary usage remains operational in practice alongside the philosophical redefinition. Beside from confusion, it also incurs the cost - of which to ask exactly where are you going toward, of those redefinitions until oblivion? Such is rather hard to answer, in which because partly of the form to base anything to be fundamental, incurs also the uncertainty that there might be the more fundamental point that disarm what we have been doing, right above. In fact, Anaximenes substituted air for water; Heraclitus, fire. Empedocles proposed all four — earth, water, air, and fire — as irreducible elements. Aristotle based his argument chiefly on the analysis of “becoming” or substantial change. Those are also pluralism, but now in the concept of elements - different categorization of substrates, of which is rather antique but intuitive, and thus giving such the baseline for which all would follow. The argument of Aristotle is also interesting. He based his argument chiefly on, paraphrased,
This is presupposing the atomic theory, in which we know that atoms, and many small sub-partitions thereof are responsible for such allowance of transitions as the ‘reference point fundamental substrate’, so to speak. But so far, those elements are still categorization of which cannot be measurable of manipulable properties. How do you quantify ‘wetness’ of water? Similarly to fire, how do you quantify the ‘fireness’ of certain elements, if they are to be derived from such? Can iron be only earthen being with certain amounts of some elemental form elsewhere? Not quite so, and indeed not so trivial. Even if in the set of no transformation, but merely successions by the annihilation of the first term - \(A\) subjects - and the creation of the second - \(B\) objects - it is still probable of such fact to say it relies less on the property baseline indicted upon. Those are external labels that we made ourselves, much to the disdain of people of the time, simply is not enough, even if it is thermodynamically interesting, anticipating something like a property-space description of phases. But in all, they are not sufficient, and one can find the breaking point anywhere one shall like to do so, and no one would be able to answer within the box of which those are to be accepted of. However, his point about conversion is right up to a certain point. Two objects in existence that are transformed from one to another, posits the fact that they are somewhat connected enough that you can morph one to another, so it means, basically that \(A\) and \(B\) must have something in common, no matter how small it is or weak it can be. This applies to also matter - you cannot transform water to iron because at the fundamental ordinary frame, they have nothing in common aside from being ‘of existence and interaction’. But, there will always be the common point - the word existence themselves. What lies after we crumble all of those objects? In one way or another, against such question, most philosophers and those of thoughts at such time, turned to hylomorphism as their saving grace.

title: 3  The map of material science
text:
1 It is of certain observation that only the concept of material aether was rejected. At all, the notion of aether was never refuted, but transubstantiated into a newer form.
Act I. (Baseline of utilization)
Material can be defined, in difference to matter, by of which it makes sense for usage of certain actor at will. That is, if such matter is of meaning to manipulate and utilization for a certain person, then it becomes material.




Act II. (Fundamentalization of derivatives on initials)
Material can be considered a set of matter, or rather, the set of all manipulable and utilized matter of interest, where its origin is fixated to become from an initial point or an initial starting substrate, for which derivations of such substrates are used to explain the classification thereof.



The underlying substrate that can take many forms, one which looks like what we call water.




If \(A\) is converted to \(B\) of a process \(T(\cdot)\), then there must exist something of common between them, without such no conversion can be done.



3.1.1 In-detail - the Aristotle’s Hylomorphism
Per the subject topic, of which more philosophical than not, in Ainsworth (2016) it was to be said that Aristotle’s hylomorphism is rather advanced for its time. The philosophical doctrine of such posits that all physical entities are compounds of matter (hyle - the material constituent or potentiality) and form (morphe or eidos - the structure essence or actuality), to explain of the material and the world.







The Hylomorphism in Aristotle’s Theory


The notion is toward what are essentially compositional thought, for Aristotle of his general ideas. Aristotle defines matter as to be ‘out of which’ something is made. For example, letters are the matter of syllables. Thus, matter is a relative term: an object counts as matter relative to something else. Clay is matter relative to a brick because a brick is made of clay, at that specific point, whereas bricks are matter relative to a brick house. Change is analyzed as a material transformation, for where matter is what undergoes a change of form. In all, it is also the relational composition that marks the strength of this approach, and perhaps even now this line of thought has only been refined, much not disappeared entirely, because of the act it allows that would be central to pretty much the way down toward atomic scale, and so on.

Act III: We presuppose matter to be relative, such that \(A\) is mater to \(B\), if \(B\) is made of \(A\). Thus, matter notion are compositional, and at such relational to a given degree.

Such relational definition of matter is rather philosophically sophisticated, if one is to claim such, which is fair for what it is worth of. For Aristotle, “matter” is not a name for some particular stuff as opposed to Thales’s thesis - but rather of the relation between objects of being. \(X\) is the matter of \(Y\) when \(Y\) is made from \(X\). This means the same stuff can be simultaneously matter, of a statue, and something that itself has matter, relative to copper and tin. There is no ultimate substratum - or if there is, of which rather an effort of such to be prime matter, it is also indeterminate as to be philosophically contentious (no one wants to seriously debate that again, for all it’s worth of).
The hierarchical, level-relative concept of material bears a striking, but not so surprising resemblance of structures to the multiscale architecture of modern materials science. At each level of the hierarchy, there is something that functions as matter to be the lower level. Then, there exists something that functions as the form binding in which makes those lower levels higher. It does not say much about what constitute the higher layer - there can be many and of extremely complex form for all the practitioner would care for, and it would still be there of the indeterminacy of such. Each level has its own characteristic form, and the explanation of properties at each level invokes the form at that level, not the form at lower levels.
Speaking of such, then why this is not utilized now? It seems that the theory can be adapted, much more general than it can be of any, which is a nice thing to have. Changing the context, and such would be complete as for a new modern explanation? Unfortunately, Aristotle’s commentators and thereof of himself, have been struggling with a quite non-trivial set of tensions, all of which testimony has been made that the structure is unstable on itself. For this, even if we ignore one of the fundamental problem of such that can be avoided by directly supervising the structure on the precision of mathematics - which would organize his anticipation of the structural-property relationship, there are still many forms in which the problem pervades of what to be presented of.

Firstly, Aristotle thinks of such as that, if one pursues this hierarchy of matter far enough downwards, Aristotle believes that one will reach the four elements. The presupposition of the four elements is simply false and conditioned of the knowledge of the time. Even if right now we presuppose one for convenience, what can we even do? There exists no determinated origin point of which we can say where will we reach. Such is to abandon the prime matter itself, but that begs the question of how far can we go down?
The theory still retains its ontological paralysis. Even if now we have been saying of the relational structure to be quite as good as it can be, the structure is paralyzed under its own statement. Suppose that \(X\) is made of \(A,B,C\). Similarly, \(Y\) is made of \(A,B,D\). Both \(X,Y\) are variations of the same copper linage, or steel, which itself is currently known as a compound. By such, the lower level of \(\{A,B,C,D\}\) contains two set of matters overlapped to give two current-layer subjects. However, they are the same under certain categorization scheme. How should we quantify this? How much of \(D\) can be settled of its form in this setting, for example? When they function in the same way, used the same way, approximately having the same setting and relational utilization to the being in usage - the anthropological baseline - what to be separated from them? Similarly, if two objects are inherently different, even though they use the exactly same set, full set of matters of which are lower-level of such, how do you compare them and distinguish them? This requires adding more information, but that might also expand if you proliferate into more complex settings, more difficult distinguishment and characterization regime, until you have quite a mess. What can we do under such?
Another tension, which have been there for a long time now, is the naturalness of the relationship between form and matter. Is the form just accidentally related to the matter, or it is essentially related to it? Can we remove it or replace it and the ‘matter’ afterward still be legitimate? The system and its frame are simply too big and too generalized, that it fails even its own test. The same structure even appears in modern materials science. The question of whether form is essential or accidental to matter is precisely the question of whether a material is defined by its composition or by its processing history. Carbon can be graphite or diamond, same matter different form, where the form is not merely accidental, but neither is the form essential to the carbon in the sense that carbon must take one form rather than another. Carbon materials can be just carbon materials, with its orientation changed, and nothing would break. Aside from the diamond.

To pull this out apart, we might as well turn our attention to the Scientific Revolution, and the subsequent Industrial-Chemical Revolutions for their insights. But let us summarize what have been observed of the all three failures, and possibly more if one wants to look enough to the picture.

3.1.1.1 Peaking - The Medieval Elaboration
Of the long-time of the Medieval period, scholasticism inherited of Aristotle through Arabic translation, primary through Avicenna and Averroes, elaborated hylomorphism into an intricate theological and metaphysical system. Those using the concept frequently distinguished between substantial form and accidental form, if one can even distinguish such from the description that is poorly operated of. For Thomas Aquinas, he argued that everything in the natural world is created by God and has specific purpose, which is revealed though both divine revelation, or natural philosophy. Such is rather characteristic of the Christian thought centred around which there are god to be, but also to set a baseline that would be rather biased, as far as we know of the present - it presupposes the purpose as already defined, of what claimed to be relational. Which is, in certain form, contradiction of sort.
Nothing much can be said about this part more than this, unfortunately. The distinguishment scheme is rather deliberate but flawed, for example,

A substantial form is what makes a thing the kind of thing it is — for a piece of bronze, its substantial form is what makes it bronze rather than tin or lead. An accidental form is a property that the thing has but could lose while remaining the same kind of thing — the shape of a bronze statue is accidental, because the bronze can be melted and recast without ceasing to be bronze.

Even if such to be extended far beyond of all creations, said statement is simply unwarranted of its determination. Tin, lead, bronze, are those that would be subjected to label, of different characteristics and structural properties in determining such. However, the determination is not discrete, there can be bronze-with-a-bit-of-tin, or bronze but designed to be at certain point, still the same substrate, but now similar to copper. And so on. Accidental form is easily to see, the shape is accidental, but also making contradiction - it can be melted, it can be into liquid form, but then would the extracted form being accidental? Why bronze just not appear in life as to be the melted form or a big blob? By then, what is even accidental anymore?



3.1.2 In-detail - the Mechanical and Chemical Revolution
Of the mechanical and chemical revolution, due of the 18th century to the down of the 19th century, a series of landmarks patents and researches were made, given the way possible of what there is to be the material science in the new dawn age. The two landmarks of the biggest kind can be served as present.

The 17th Century foundation of the mechanical philosophy of Descartes, Gassendi, Boyle, and Newton performed a philosophical operation on the concept of material, that has shaped material ever since. We cannot truly comprehend of what the consequences are, but it would like to be thought of still being worked out, even by modern mechanisms. There are many concepts evolved of the time, for Boyle to be individual bit or formational characteristics, of size, shape, orientation, order and textures, being matter completely passive and inert. For Descartes, the notion of duality took place, for where there exists again the inertness of the subject matter, then comes the exclusion of all psychic characteristic of which earlier of history being framed to be material nature, and forces physical nature to be inert and devoid of sources of activity on its own - such distinction is rather very strong, and legacy of such thought remains in the entire body of physics still of present.


Let us, for a moment, reveal Act IV.

Act IV:
Instead of asking matter versus material. Let us ask. They are the same. But what constitutes them?

Such would be relevant throughout the latter sections itself, and conclude the major act that we would be seeing. And this collapse, would incur the cost that current theory are still paying, though the institution with its pocket are rather generous. That said, I am not so sure of the science itself.

In such, would rather to be said, the theory that we know right now of the Newtonian mechanics, bears the most responsibility of the transition. Newtonian physics, in general, inherited and fleshed out positions of Boyle, and Descartes, of which to be the physical reality being acted upon, for those mechanical philosophies stated imply the advocation of corpuscular structures, and microstructure constitution. In retrospect, individual ‘small parts’ arrange themselves into corpuscular structure that gives a substance its various properties. Different corpuscular structure account for different substances and different properties. As far as we consider, Boyle’s corpuscular theory is, an second early version, after Aristotle’s, of the structure-property relationship, where the microstructure of the corpuscles determines the properties of the bulk material. While mechanical in nature, as it relies on size, shape, arrangement, motions - replacing form by geometry - essentially 2, it is still a granted substantial contribution, for the elimination of any teleological or dispositional explanation from material science. Matter now does not have indicted meaning of the higher-order being, nor the existence thereof for such matter to be aware, as for it to gain purposes. But rather, it makes due of what there is, for which components it shares of existence in the form of becoming.
2 It is good to stop and note that, even of the current form, the philosophical question of what to be the form of the object is still under heavy debate. Though, as it currently stands, it would be a nice change of pace to stop and transfer it to another framework itself, rather than sticking to such term.Newtonian physics patched up the operational ideal of such form separation by co-author of sort the position similar to what Boyle and Descartes have done (post-instantiation, in one way of speaking), by removing the object from its force inside his developed analytical framework. A force is exerted, and of its foundation if none of such force are at present, the state of the object simple stays the same, so to speak. The object becomes potential, of properties, of mass, of momentum, whatever, of what to be the properties and dynamics that follows. One subtle consequence of such, is thus before any interaction can be made, they are effectively of the expression, to be decoupled from each other and bear no relevance from either side. It foreshadows an aspect - to truly see properties of object, there exists the requirement of interaction per specification. This means, in simple term, that by decoupling the two, you are now asking the question: how do you see it? Of course, you cannot objectively see it, as per definition of ‘giving out’ properties require you to touch it, ordinarily speaking, or probe it under experiments, strictly speaking. But this on itself is an act of interaction and methodological intervention. Such is, there is no view of the pure potential aside from those you presuppose to be minimal, such is also how most of the time we approximate subjects - negligible, supposing air frictions as such, supposing interaction does not move the objects, so on so forth. There exists, as such scheme on itself, any way to get properties of an object further than the identification that such object exists, which implicitly requires subtle interaction - either by its deformation and illumination of a luminiferous object toward us that we can see of its existence, or by various interaction of which finally we obtain of the relevant resultant of such. In a sense, surprisingly speaking, existence-identification is already a form of measurement, which at best of the viewport, there is no pre-observational baseline at all. You would either have to get the snapshot of time, and presuppose linearity or uniformity of behaviours, and predict the previous state, while simultaneously the future states, where states here is defined operationally simple as the snapshot in which the being, under certain description, contains certain amount of information that describe it of which quantity or of what properties. Conjuring such, the thesis is breached - there is no view from nowhere onto the object’s properties. Every observation is already an intervention, the mechanical philosophy’s dream of reading off fixed corpuscular properties hits the wall of its own dynamics, by its own language, of its own virtue.
Simplification, as we called of such, also appears in the corpuscular itself. There exists the fundamental problem at that stage with the notion of continuity and discreteness, of such is born out of the philosophy in which we are to say, each form of object presupposes the layer below it to provide ‘small components’ that would form the bricks and mortars of the house. However, such is rather unclear how to dissect of it, rather than to presuppose that there exists the absolute form at the lower end of the spectrum, to be the prime matter, as of such returned to Aristotle baseline. But every baseline can be reduced to such as to ask, would there be any lower-level substrates that support also the prime matter? How would that be verified of said descriptions? In a sense, point mass is a notion used in Newtonian physics to hand-wave such notion - by making concentration to a singular, dimensionless point, forgoing any volumetric uncertainty where one now introduces the volume approximation, and both the volume of the corpuscle itself. But that does not indict that reality has to be this way, but rather again another simplification of approximation of reality. We can see this, actually, when we move onto rigid-object dynamics, where one again uses those point masses constructions for the rigid object. However, density of such can only be gauged, up to a certain point, and the point-mass object under such description is enumerative-wise large, \(N\to \infty\) if able as to fully fill in all the admissible space created by the model. By then, a simplification scheme is again made, returning to the volumetric sub-volume, on and on and on, until that we redefine point mass as to be the relative minimal volumetric space. But doing so inadvertently contradicts both the baseline, and the certainty of partition. The corpuscular itself is then not corpuscular, and its form is conditioned on the volumetric space of the larger system, where now the rigid object stays in such form because of other ‘corpuscle’. Which is a rather roundabout problem of the structure itself 3, and ironically, which is precisely what the mechanical philosophy was trying to escape from in Aristotle - relational, context-dependent identity. Another dilemma is also to break the prime matter entirely, because now, once you allow the point mass to become a minimal sub-volume, you immediately face the question of how to partition the volume. Different partitioning schemes give different “corpuscles” for the same object. Which partition is the real one? The framework has no answer because the partition is chosen by the modeller and of which designers are there for computational convenience, not discovered in the object. The corpuscles are as much considered of being artifacts of the description as features of reality it presupposes.
3 Surprisingly, as we soon will expand of the modern science section, quantum physics is better only at this aspect - such simplification is performed better and more honest than what we have seen as collapse in here.
The Mechanical Revolution, or First Industrial Revolution, of which mechanized textile production, mining, iron-making, transport, and many, is one such factor where the role of material science drifted. Certainly, of (Mohajan 2019),(Sharma 2022),(Mitrović 2022),(Watt 1769),(Klein and Lefèvre 2007),(Taylor 2007), they depended on new materials and on evolving ways of thinking about materials, in the same time such philosophical intervention are made. Coke-smelted iron (Abraham Darby’s patent) provided cast iron in abundance never seen before; Darby’s Coalbrookdale works cast over 100 Newcomen steam-engine cylinders by 1758, showing iron production scaling with steam technology. By 1779 Darby’s descendants built one of the first cast-iron bridges (Ironbridge) and in 1802 the first steam locomotive, illustrating that new metalworking methods enabled entirely new structures. As materials became central, scientific study of them expanded: 18th-century metallurgists (e.g. Réaumur, Grignon) began examining crystal structures in iron and alloy behaviour (see (Taylor 2007)). Historians by then, note that chemists and engineers started treating substances as defined “objects of inquiry” with measurable properties. The question came out from the mechanical era is rather distinct, as to almost abandon the ontology into the question to the classification problem and identification itself, to metallurgy, to characterization, and many of such are detrimental as the workhorse of the revolution itself. Out of every patent and revolution landmarks stated, only one single work of James Watt to be the introduction of the core thermodynamic concepts. Even then, the concept itself is highly operational - it presupposes the function and bears no mind to the separation of matter and properties. Here, they are both the embodiment of the same object - the subject ‘matter’, having both properties, and of its matter functional states. Now, objects would be characterized by their shape and forms, mass, interactions, behaviours, boiling points, operational quantities in operation of interaction. We are to then admit that as is, the separation simply does not make any sense operationally, because an object at rest, similar to what Smith used to characterize of the old philosophy - relational to the worker and industrial machinery. How that is reconciled to the crux of Newtonian mechanics, which secretly or not presupposed the latter is itself an interesting question, but not the main one at this point. The question now turns to the final pillar of which to explain, even if operationally, what can the compositions to the macroscopic down to the microscopic be of? The answer, of course, at this point, would be atoms of the time, but that requires a separated revolution on its own.

The question here is valid. At this stage of the scientific body, the matter-properties distinction is operationally meaningless. What is of use to think about an object for its matter, and for its properties to be different, while working with them, they seem to be one? Object is also only accessible via interaction, as far as we see of what we established. Corpuscles again introduced the uncertainty and arbitrary partition dependency again, after works. The identity itself is replaced of Aristotle precondition of relationalism - you cannot sufficiently determine the ground at where and of what, without the circular circus being relevant to the picture. The question now that

What kind of theory could restore determinacy without reintroducing naive ontology? Can such theory restore or at least attempt to, of object identity and classification after the collapse of intrinsic properties, without reintroducing arbitrary metaphysical primitives, or not?

The solution, of the mechanical elaboration, ironically, operationally collapsed the matter/properties separation that the mechanical philosophy had just spent a century carefully constructing. Granted, we do not actually know of it if the matter-properties ontology is physically relevant and provides us with a schematic of such for understanding closer to what we presuppose as the true object itself. But collapsing such for the purpose of operational success is rather hiding the debt away, until we finally reach the ladder rung where those questions are again valid. The only problem within such way, is that while the revolution that the mechanical philosophy made possible - industrialization - produced a material practice that implicitly contradicted the mechanical philosophy’s own ontology, it is worse that such action remain hidden inside its own framework, just as we have mentioned earlier during the Newtonian cascade, of the separation itself, the theory being successful but hiding the uncomfortable question about relativeness and inference, of which later would be the absolute boundary that the frame fails, thus implicitly leads to the new theory about the restricted frame on itself. And so, where the frame of the mechanical nature is failing secretly, what is holding it together is the demand for the atomic theory, which is to supplant of the chemical revolution. In all, the purpose of the Chemical Revolution is the forced hand of precision, where theory comes to demand more and more grounding of what to be invariant, unchanged, of identity. And, it is to note trivial of present, it is not the first attempt (or maybe it is), and also not the final answer.

Due of Antoine Lavoisier’s chemical revolution, of which is the central part to overturn phlogiston theory, sparked the newer term of which now we saw as the modern chemical science era. The analysis is rather delicate, and should be taken into consideration. Due of history, before Lavoisier made his progresses, Georg Ernst Stahl as the German chemist of the old day, proposed what we now call as phlogiston, of which being the intangible substance released from fermentation, combustion and relevant processes of the kind (note that this is deliberately arbitrary). Thus, every object or matter in consideration of a specific interaction process, forgoing the question of matter-property but to treat it as plain object of distinguishment, to be of specific amount of \(\mathrm{Ph}(A)\) for object class \(A\). During combustion, then for example, phlogiston was thought to be expelled into air, resulting in a dephlogisticated residue, such as wood ash (see more in here). On the surface, it seems probable, as during such transformation process, there exists the residue of which we can see of the transformation being \(A\to B+ C\), where \(C\) is the ash and \(B\) is the product (we are doing process schema here). The question of how \(C\) were there, in the first place, is the Aristotle question asked of the lower level, and here Stahl predicated it with phlogiston. How Lavoisier disproved it? Well, not by operating within the framework itself, because the framework is sound in its question of deliverance - there must be something that give rise to such combustion residue - the residue does not really look like \(A\), nor it is similar to what \(B\) produced. So there are external factors, or, in this case, another internal factor of itself in the subject that would only be released by interaction in the kind of combustion (here, is the interaction picture). Instead, Lavoisier attempted the experiment to show that combustion involves oxygen that transform the subject itself. This targets a rather simple case - metal rust, where the object actually during the process increases of volume instead of reducing, of which supposedly reducing in phlogiston during the process set up a kind of internal conservation law within itself - that phlogiston + matter would stay the same instead; which, evidently, is not the case. As of such, we have the following empirical refutation of which one made to disprove at such boundary.


Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, the most prominent antiphlogistonist, believed that calcination produced a weight gain in metals because something in the air combined with the metal. He repeated the experiments of Priestley, interpreting the change in the lead calx as the loss of a gas into the air. This explanation solved the problem of weight gain experienced by metals when calcinated: Lavoisier reasoned that the same gas that a calcinated metal released had bonded to it when it was originally calcinated, and the weight of the gas had been added to the weight of the pure metal at that time. Lavoisier named this new gas “oxygen.” Although Lavoisier was never able to dissuade Priestley from believing in phlogiston, he did convince most other chemists of his day that the theory needed to be discarded. 4
4 Even then, we can see that not even Lavoisier can convince the phlogistonists such as Priestley himself. His experiment is rather sound, however despite popular beliefs and what to be considered of the narrative refutation. In one, he heated some calx of lead (mercuric oxide) in a closed container and found that the air released by the calx caused a candle to burn more vigorously and that a mouse placed in the container could breathe longer than when placed in normal air. Priestley called the air inside the container “dephlogisticated air”: He assumed that, by heating lead calx, he had removed phlogiston from normal air and caused it to be reabsorbed by the calx. In fact, rather than removing something from the air, Priestley had added to it when the heated mercuric oxide gave off oxygen. Without the knowledge nor the realization of the breaking case, one would have to see that the evidences inside, suggested phlogiston to be rather right.
The ontological baseline now shifted, where phlogiston is actually the substance air of which combine to give the effect a stable cause. The question again shifted toward, what is even air? How would air combines with the matter of metal to produce combustion? The layer is now clarified quite a bit, as for there must be something smaller that make up both the metal, and both the air, for them to interact and give rise to residue, albeit of the same mass for both as it is. It is also a rather early entry to the concept of entropy and energy transformation - if we are to have same mass, accumulated throughout air giving in to give rise to rust and so on, then during the process of burning, we lose the torch and of the fire soon fade. Then, what is transformed, and what was lost during that process? Such question would be answered later, or rather not, as the body of science already gave its way toward it, and we should not reinvent nor reinterpreting it, lest of the space available in the discourse such is this small section. That said, we now have the conservation law of Mass, where now mass of constituent, actually can be traced to specific interaction partners of the process, not merely attribute more to what there exists. Such is also again, a problem of which still surfaces as of the modern context - how do you characterize materials good enough to get that distinction, and should that be answered, many would be elucidated of the process. For now, the revolution points itself to the quality of which that can be qualified, for the first time in many decades of works.
Let us end the section by taking on the implications thereof for this linage of itself, and of the chemical revolution in its entirety. Namely, the technological ‘marvel’ thereof. For what to be seen from (American Chemical Society (ACS) n.d.), (American Chemical Society (ACS) n.d.b), (Flavell-While 2011), (Roebuck n.d. / c. 1746), (Encyclopaedia Britannica Editors n.d.d), (Encyclopaedia Britannica Editors n.d.b), (Encyclopaedia Britannica Editors n.d.a), and of (Encyclopaedia Britannica Editors n.d.c) for what history preserved of intentions and records, the Chemical Revolution indeed made the depth of how materials were to be defined, albeit with the same constraints we set above.

Klein & Lefèvre show that 18th-century chemists developed a new ontology of substances: they identified and categorized “pure chemical substances” by composition. For example, air was re-ontologized into oxygen, nitrogen, etc. Traditional “affinity tables” of the pre-1789 era (organizing substances by reaction affinities) gave way to Lavoisier’s Tableau de nomenclature chimique (1787), classifying substances by elemental makeup5.
5 Again, we note the lower-level commitment here as non-trivial. It will recur in later organization.
Much can be said of the later work, i.e. Dalton’s atomic theory to enhance such, and also to explain of what to be said from our analysis, to be of the following incursion. The atomic theory helped in the way of the forced hand of description, during which it proposed:

All matter is composed of extremely small indivisible particles called atoms.
Atoms, of a given element are identical in size, mass and other properties. Atoms of different elements differ in size, mass and other properties. Such is to say, we have the atomic species, or, elements.
Atoms cannot be subdivided, created or destroyed. That is, atoms of an element are not changed into atoms of a different element during chemical reaction.
Atoms of different elements combined in simple whole number ratios to form chemical compounds.
In chemical reactions, atoms are combined, separated or rearranged.
In a given compound, the relative number and kind of atoms are constant.

Supported by again, Lavoisier, alongside the set of empirical law on conservation of mass, the law of definite proportions, and law of constant composition, and, lastly, multiple proportions. What is said, however, is that the apparent contradiction of the grounding to shut down the lower-level constituent, has been settled. What to be lower than the atom itself is not in the question but delegated into impossibility - we simply cannot reach. In a sense, and of the period, such worked spectacularly within the domain where such grounding is applicable. History, however, writes itself. And so far, before we move on to diagnose the failure of such, we are set one account that by virtue of our currently knowledge only, would be contingent to the realization. The quark was being idle.
For industrial chemistry itself, the new chemistry indeed gained operational success, especially of large-scale chemical manufacturing process. The two often cited prospect arose to be as followed,

Sulphuric acid: John Roebuck’s lead-chamber process (1746) allowed bulk acid production. By lining wooden reaction chambers with lead, Roebuck’s method produced concentrated sulphuric acid at far lower cost. This massive supply of acid fuelled textiles, metallurgy and later fertilizers.
Soda ash: Nicolas Leblanc devised a process (patented 1791) to make soda from common salt and sulphuric acid. Leblanc’s method “turned soda production from nothingness to a major industry”. His 1791 patent was lauded as “very superior” in economy and purity. Mid-19th century production reached ~400,000 tons/year. These early chemical plants (sulphuric acid, soda) were among the first examples of the modern chemical industry.

AT last, from 1780s, the shift has been to be foundational - where substances were identified, individuated, ordered per specification of certain dialect, and classed on the basis of their composition. What seemed to be mundane and non-trivial, by such effect, are now the central of studies in the search for the elemental substrates underlying typically can be said of almost everything that can be made of in nature. The ontological shift is now fair bit better - while the lower-level still retains the inherent grounding question, such is to say the layer worked far better than anticipated, one part no small of its simplification and enunciation for which materials are identified under empirical analysis isolated enough to trivialize complexity, as it is certainly one would not want his chainsaw to be reek of rust when he first began the journey into lumbering. In a sense, chemists started regarding matter, and materials thereof, as a set of chemically defined substances. The shift occurred in matter. The material does not.

4.1 Reframing artificial intelligence
Now, that can be rather coincidental for me to have observed the utilization and push toward using artificial intelligence, or system coined of such, in the process of analysis and material identification. In general, what we have been calling as AI, should not be justified or rather identified as such. Moreover, especially employed in physics, should we call them AI, it would be a rather deliberate degradation of the term itself, toward which the subjects of consideration in the physical field of science are employing those for structural recovery, autonomous pattern-based extraction and thereof, not exactly ‘AI’. Thence, a technical reframing and introduction might be needed, and that is exactly this section on itself.

3.2 Modern scientific theories on material sciences
It is rather undermining to start the section about what to be said of material science to be an elaboration from what industrial and chemical revolution are to be of. Almost arrogantly, we settled on the rhetoric that the history of material science of the modern time only starts here. What we have done in the 20th and 21st century would be in the same time bracket, and of which there are no ‘modern’ in the sense of what we usually claim, but the modern here had been there for more than two hundred years.
